bull.b: Repeated piloted transition flights and two full-scale prototypes provide tangible evidence that Vertical is converting its aircraft concept into a testable platform. Higher flight-test capacity can accelerate engineering learning, support regulatory engagement, and reduce technical execution risk over the next several quarters.

The breadth of technology, infrastructure, customer, and regulatory relationships strengthens Vertical’s ability to develop a complete advanced-air-mobility ecosystem. These collaborations can improve certification readiness, operational integration, and commercial credibility beyond the aircraft itself.

Progress toward dedicated assembly and expanded battery capacity indicates a transition from prototype development toward industrial readiness. Building internal production capability and increasing battery throughput could support certification work, early aircraft deliveries, and future electric or hybrid variants.

bear.b: The absence of meaningful revenue and continuing operating deficits show that Vertical has not yet demonstrated commercial scale or self-sustaining unit economics. Until certification and customer commitments translate into sales, earnings power remains dependent on successful execution of a capital-intensive development program.

bear.t: High cash burn and funding dependence
bear.b: Persistent negative operating and free cash flow requires Vertical to secure additional external capital while it develops and certifies its aircraft. High projected outflows reduce financial flexibility, increase dependence on financing conditions, and could constrain the pace of testing, industrialization, and commercialization.

Moving type certification to 2029 extends the period before meaningful commercial deliveries and revenue can begin. The delay also prolongs cash consumption and leaves more time for regulatory, technical, or execution setbacks to increase funding requirements and defer the company’s transition to operating scale.
